Superstition
sū-pẽr-stĭsh´ŭn
n. (religion misdirected; reverence given to what has no claim to it; rendering Greek deisidaimonia)
Latin superstitio, literally a standing over — the awe of the man who stands transfixed before what he fears. The Greek of Acts 25:19 is deisidaimonia, fear of the divinities, a word that can mean religiousness or dread according to the speaker.

Biblical Definition

Superstition is reverence bestowed where God has not placed it. Festus described the dispute between Paul and the Jews as “certain questions against him of their own superstition, and of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive” (Act 25:19) — a pagan magistrate's dismissal of a religion he could not follow. Paul at Athens used the kindred word of the city itself: “Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious” (Act 17:22), and then preached the unknown God they had an altar to. The Lord's diagnosis of religion gone wrong is the standing one: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines superstition as excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unnecessary scruples; belief in the direct agency of superior powers in extraordinary events; false religion; excessive nicety.

expand to see more

SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unnecessary scruples in the observance of religious rites not commanded, or of points of minor importance.

2. A reverence of beings not proper objects of reverence; false religion; false worship.

3. Rite or practice proceeding from excess of scruples in religion.

4. Excessive nicety; scrupulous exactness.

Key Scripture

Act 25:19 — "But had certain questions against him of their own superstition, and of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive."

Act 17:22 — "Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious."

Mat 15:9 — "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men."

Col 2:23 — "Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh."

Gal 4:10 — "Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years."

Modern Corruption

Superstition is imagined as the vice of the ignorant, and Scripture finds it in the temple, in Athens, and in the churches of Galatia.

expand to see more

The word is now used almost entirely of the uneducated — charms, ladders, black cats — and Scripture never uses it that way. Superstition in the Bible is a disorder of religion itself, and it appears among the most careful worshippers on record. The Pharisees washed, tithed the herbs of the garden, and counted paces on the sabbath, and the Lord's verdict on the whole apparatus was that they worshipped in vain, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men. Superstition is not too little religion. It is religion aimed at something God did not command, performed with a scruple He never asked for.

Galatians 4:10 is the form it takes in a Christian congregation: ye observe days, and months, and times, and years — and Paul's response is not amusement but alarm, “I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain.” The observance was religious, sincere, and biblical in its raw materials, since the days and months came out of Moses; and it was a return to the weak and beggarly elements, because it was being kept as a ground of standing. That is the exact mechanism. A practice becomes superstitious not when it is old or ceremonious but when a man's peace begins to rest on it.

Athens shows the other end of the range, and Paul's tone there is worth learning. He calls the city too superstitious, and then walks its streets, reads its altars, quotes its poets, and preaches the resurrection from the one inscription that admitted ignorance. He does not despise the impulse; he redirects it. Superstition is the religious instinct running without revelation, and the answer to it is not less reverence but a right object, which is why the sermon ends at a Man whom God hath raised from the dead.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek deisidaimonia (G1175), fear of the divine, religiousness or superstition; deisidaimonesteros (G1174), too superstitious; ethelothreskeia (G1479), will-worship; mataios (G3152), vain.

expand to see more

Greek deisidaimonia (G1175) — superstition, religion; Acts 25:19 only.

Greek deisidaimonesteros (G1174) — too superstitious, very religious; Acts 17:22 only.

Greek maten sebontai (G3155, G4576) — in vain they worship; Matthew 15:9, Mark 7:7.

Usage

"“Questions against him of their own superstition” — a Roman governor's word for the gospel."

"“Ye men of Athens… too superstitious” — the instinct redirected, not despised."

"“Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years” — the form it takes in a church."
